content: 1. The coronary anatomy is divided into specific segments to identify the location of the culprit artery. 2. Segment 0: No lesion is present angiographically with a stenosis greater than 50%. 3. Segment 1: The proximal right coronary artery (R1) extends from the origin of the right coronary artery to the first of the three longest acute marginal branches. 4. Segment 2: The mid-right coronary artery (R2) extends from the origin of the first acute marginal branch to the origin of the third acute marginal branch. 5. Segment 3: The distal right coronary artery (R3) extends from the origin of the third acute marginal branch to the origin of the posterior descending artery. 6. Segment 4: The right posterolateral artery (R4), also known as the right retroventricular artery, is the distal continuation of the right coronary artery after the origin of the posterior descending artery. It often has an inverted U shape and gives rise to the AV nodal branch. It supplies blood to the right posterior and right inferior arteries in large right-dominant anatomy, only the right inferior branch in small right-dominant anatomy, and is absent in left or balanced dominant systems. 7. Segments 5, 6, 7: The acute marginal arteries (A1, A2, A3) are the three longest branches arising from the right coronary artery, supplying the right ventricular wall. They are numbered from proximal to distal. 8. Segment 8: The right posterior descending artery (RD), also called the right posterior interventricular artery, runs in the posterior interventricular groove in all but left-dominant systems. It supplies septal perforator branches and is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 9. Segment 9: The right inferior artery (RI) arises from the fourth segment of the right coronary artery and supplies the inferior wall. In small right-dominant anatomy, it is the distal-most branch of the right coronary artery, while in large right-dominant anatomy, it arises proximal to the origin of the right posterior artery. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 10. Segment 10: The right posterior artery (RP) is the distal-most branch of the right coronary artery, present only in large right-dominant systems. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 11. Segment 11: The left main coronary artery (LM) extends from the origin of the left coronary artery to its bifurcation into the left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex (LCx) arteries. 12. Segment 12: The proximal left anterior descending artery (L1) extends from the bifurcation of the left main coronary artery to the origin of the first septal branch. 13. Segment 13: The mid-left anterior descending artery (L2) extends from the origin of the first septal branch to the origin of the third septal branch. 14. Segment 14: The distal left anterior descending artery (L3) extends from the origin of the third septal branch to the apex of the left ventricle. If no third septal branch is present, this segment begins halfway between the first septal branch and the apex of the left ventricle. 15. Segment 15: The left anterior descending artery terminus on the inferior wall (L4) is the continuation of the LAD beyond the apex of the left ventricle in cases where the LAD is a wrap-around variant. 16. Segment 16: The first diagonal artery (D1) is the first of the three longest branches off the LAD, supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. 17. Segment 17: The second diagonal artery (D2) is the second of the three longest branches off the LAD, supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. 18. Segment 18: The third diagonal artery (D3) is the third of the three longest branches off the LAD, supplying the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle. In a right anterior oblique (RAO) projection, this artery often arises where the LAD angles toward the apex. 19. Segments 19, 20, 21: The septal arteries (S1, S2, S3) are the three largest branches off the LAD, supplying the interventricular septum. 20. Segment 22: The median ramus (MR), also called the intermedius ramus, is an artery that originates between the LAD and LCx. When present, the left main artery trifurcates into the LAD, LCx, and MR. It is grouped with the LCx unless otherwise specified by trial protocols. 21. Segment 23: The proximal circumflex artery (C1) extends from the origin of the LCx off the left main artery to the origin of the first marginal or obtuse marginal branch. If a second obtuse marginal branch is present and the first marginal branch is absent, the C1–C2 transition is defined as halfway between the origin of the LCx and the origin of the second obtuse marginal branch. 22. Segment 24: The mid-circumflex artery (C2) extends from the origin of the first marginal or obtuse marginal branch to the origin of the second marginal or obtuse marginal branch. If a second obtuse marginal branch is present and the first marginal branch is absent, the C1–C2 transition is defined as halfway between the origin of the LCx and the origin of the second obtuse marginal branch. If the first obtuse marginal branch is present and the second marginal branch is absent, the C2–C3 transition is defined as halfway between the first obtuse marginal branch and the end of C3. 23. Segment 25: The distal circumflex artery (C3) extends from the origin of the second marginal or obtuse marginal branch to the termination of the LCx in large right-dominant anatomy or to the origin of the circumflex posterior branch (CP) in all other dominance patterns. 24. Segment 26: The left posterolateral artery (C4) is the distal continuation of the LCx in left-dominant or balanced systems. It supplies the left posterior descending artery and circumflex inferior artery in left-dominant systems and only the circumflex inferior artery in balanced systems. 25. Segment 27: The circumflex posterior artery (CP) originates at the distal end of the third segment of the LCx at the border of the inferior and lateral left ventricular walls. It is one of the three longest branches supplying the inferior wall of the heart when present. 26. Segment 28: The circumflex inferior artery (CI) arises from the junction between C3 and C4 and supplies the inferior wall. In balanced dominant anatomy, it is the distal-most branch of the LCx, while in left-dominant anatomy, it arises proximal to the origin of the left posterior descending artery. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 27. Segment 29: The left posterior descending artery (CD) is the distal continuation of the LCx in left-dominant systems. It travels in the interventricular groove and supplies septal perforators at the base of the heart. It is one of the three longest branches on the inferior wall of the heart when present. 28. Segments 30, 31, 32: The marginal arteries (M1, M2, M3) are the three longest branches off the LCx, supplying the lateral wall of the left ventricle unless a large branching vessel dominates the lateral wall. When a large dominating artery is present, it is called an obtuse marginal artery. These marginal arteries are numbered from proximal (M1) to distal (M3). 29. Segments 33, 37, 41: The obtuse marginal arteries (OM1–OM3) are large branching arteries that dominate the lateral left ventricular wall. They consist of anterior and posterior branches that share a common trunk. These branches may substitute for the first and second marginal branches (or the second and third marginal branches), although a first (or third) marginal branch may still be present. No more than one obtuse marginal artery may be present. The obtuse marginal artery is further specified as OM1, OM2, or OM3 depending on its origin relative to the usual origins of the first, second, and third marginal arteries. 30. Segments 36, 40, 44: The obtuse marginal trunk (OT) is the common trunk connecting the anterior and posterior branches of an obtuse marginal artery to the LCx. As no more than one obtuse marginal artery may be present, the OT is not numbered. Segment 36 corresponds to OM1/OT, segment 40 to OM2/OT, and segment 44 to OM3/OT. 31. Segments 34, 38, 42: The anterior branch of the obtuse marginal artery (OA) is the anterior branch of a large branching vessel dominating the lateral left ventricular wall. As no more than one obtuse marginal artery may be present, the OA is not numbered. Segment 34 corresponds to OM1/OA, segment 38 to OM2/OA, and segment 42 to OM3/OA. 32. Segments 35, 39, 43: The posterior branch of the obtuse marginal artery (OP) is the posterior branch of a large branching vessel dominating the lateral left ventricular wall. As no more than one obtuse marginal artery may be present, the OP is not numbered. Segment 35 corresponds to OM1/OP, segment 39 to OM2/OP, and segment 43 to OM3/OP. 33. Segment 45: The saphenous vein graft to the LAD (SVGLAD). 34. Segment 46: The saphenous vein graft to the circumflex artery (SVGCX). 35. Segment 47: The saphenous vein graft to the right coronary artery (SVGRCA). 36. Segment 48: The saphenous vein graft to the posterior descending artery (SVGPDA). 37. Segment 49: The saphenous vein graft to the obtuse marginal artery (SVGOM). 38. Segment 50: The saphenous vein graft to the diagonal artery (SVGD). 39. Segment 51: The left internal mammary artery to the LAD (LIMA). 40. Segment 52: The right internal mammary artery to the LAD (RIMA). Definitions of Segmental Coronary Anatomy 1. If a lesion occurs at a branch point, it is considered part of the proximal vessel adjacent to the branch point. 2. If a lesion involves both the parent vessel and a side branch at a branch point (e.g., a trifurcation lesion or Mercedes Benz emblem lesion involving the LAD and the origin of a diagonal branch), the larger parent vessel is defined as the culprit.
